endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: The research and operational teams ran COMPOSER in silent mode before activation, used a phased go-live, and established a structured clinician feedback loop in which alert disposition (acted on, deferred, or overridden) was logged and reviewed by the development team to recalibrate thresholds and retrain staff where needed.

evidence.title: Clinical acceptance of a digital health clinical decision support algorithm for children in Tanzania and Rwanda: A mixed-method and before-after analysis from the DYNAMIC study
evidence.effect: Adapting algorithms based on findings from overridden or rejected diagnoses led to improved acceptance for some diagnoses.
evidence.quote: A before–after analysis showed improved acceptance for some diagnoses following adaptations.

evidence.title: Academic Detailing to Enhance Adoption of Clinical Decision Support for Patients at Risk of Opioid Overdose
evidence.effect: Reviewing alert dispositions to deliver targeted emails to under-responding providers increased the prescription-to-alert ratio by 41.3%.
evidence.quote: The second intervention resulted in an increased prescription-to-alert ratio from 9.3 to 50.6%, an absolute increase of 41.3% when comparing the nearly 8 months before and after the emails were sent (95% CI: 36.9-45.7%, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Sisyphus' Alert: The Uphill Struggle to Improve Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis Clinical Decision Support
evidence.effect: Post-launch modifications based on feedback did not significantly decrease the 88% rate of alerts being dismissed without action.
evidence.quote: Modifications also did not cause a significant decrease in how frequently the alert was dismissed without further action being taken (88%).

evidence.title: Don’t set and forget: Optimising Digital Early Warning Tools through upgrade and evaluation
evidence.effect: stakeholders reported experiencing issues with alert fatigue while using the digital early warning tool
evidence.quote: Stakeholder focus groups and surveys identified a lack of awareness of specific functionality, issues with alert fatigue, technical challenges with the system, the need for training and concerns around over-reliance on the system by junior staff.

evidence.title: Examining clinician choice to follow-up (or not) on automated notifications of medication non-adherence by clinical decision support systems
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Proportion of CDSS non-adherence flags clinicians followed up versus not followed up
evidence.effect: 260 (78%) of flags were Not Followed-up; 71 (22%) were Followed-up. Anti-depressant flags were less likely to be followed up than Anti-Psychotic and Anxiolytic flags (p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: The majority of clients were Not Followed-up (n = 260; 78%; Followed-up: n = 71; 22%).

evidence.title: Single-center outcomes of artificial intelligence in management of pulmonary embolism and pulmonary embolism response team activation
evidence.venue: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
evidence.outcome: Alert burden and notification fatigue from AI auto-detection notifications to PERT
evidence.effect: High rate of discordant AI auto-detection (71.5% false positives) raised concerns of increased PERT workload, alarm/notification fatigue, and automation bias; direct notification did not improve PERT triage efficacy.
evidence.quote: This can lead to increased workloads for PERT consultants, alarm/notification fatigue, and automation bias.
evidence.sample_unit: CTPA exams flagged by AI as suspected PE

evidence.title: Sisyphus' Alert: The Uphill Struggle to Improve Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis Clinical Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Alert dismissal without orders after iterative logic changes
evidence.effect: Alert dismissed without further action 88% of the time; modifications did not significantly decrease dismissal; firing rose from 53.8 to 61 per 1,000 patient days.
evidence.quote: Modifications also did not cause a significant decrease in how frequently the alert was dismissed without further action being taken (88%).

evidence.title: Clinical decision support to aid in diagnosis of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
evidence.outcome: Clinician response (diagnostic testing) to CDS advisory in highest-risk patients
evidence.effect: 14 of 26 patients with 4Ts scores ≥6 did not undergo HIT diagnostic testing despite the advisory; eight had possible complications from undiagnosed HIT.
evidence.quote: Fourteen of the 26 patients with 4Ts scores ≥6 did not undergo diagnostic testing for HIT despite the CDS advisory, and eight had possible complications from undiagnosed HIT.

evidence.title: Long-Term Impact of a Clinical Decision Support System on Potassium Prescription Safety in a Brazilian Tertiary-Care Hospital: A Retrospective Observational Study (2006-2023)
evidence.venue: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
evidence.outcome: Rate and trend of CDSS blocked prescription attempts and persistent near misses
evidence.effect: 38,961 of 90,741 prescriptions (42.9%) triggered blocked attempts with upward trend (β = 20.4, p < 0.001); near misses median 27.4% (IQR 17.5-32.2), suggesting alert fatigue and overreliance
evidence.quote: After CDSS implementation, 90,741 potassium prescriptions were submitted, of which 38,961 (42.9%) triggered CDSS blocked attempts, showing a consistent upward trend (β = 20.4, p < 0.001).

commentary.bottom_line: Three uncontrolled before-after studies in live deployments report that reviewing alert dispositions was followed by higher alert acceptance or response in two cases and by no significant change in an 88% dismissal rate in the third. These studies suggest the practice is feasible, but they cannot show that disposition review caused the gains.

perspectives.view: All three tests of the practice are before-after studies without a comparison group. Under GRADE these start at low certainty and drop further for risk of bias and inconsistent results. One reported a 41.3% rise in the prescription-to-alert ratio, one reported improved acceptance for some diagnoses, and one found no significant fall in dismissals.

Hazard studies show that alert dispositions affect patients. In one, 14 of 26 highest-risk patients did not receive HIT testing despite an advisory, and eight had possible complications. Another found that 78% of non-adherence flags were not followed up. Disposition logs could reveal such gaps, but no included study shows that logging reduced harm events.

At one site, iterative logic changes left 88% of alerts dismissed while firing rose from 53.8 to 61 per 1,000 patient days. A potassium CDSS blocked 42.9% of prescriptions, and the blocking rate trended upward. These results suggest that disposition review may need to reduce alert volume as well as revise alert logic.

The targeted-email approach, applied across 2,161 providers, suggests one low-cost response to disposition data. The Tanzania and Rwanda study adapted algorithms from override findings across 27,593 consultations. Neither study reported the staff time or cost of reviewing dispositions, so resource needs at scale remain unknown.

One test took place in Tanzania and Rwanda, and the other two did not report their country or population. No test reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. It is therefore unknown whether override patterns, or the response to disposition review, differ for these groups.

AI pulmonary embolism notifications had a 71.5% false positive rate, which raised concern about fatigue among response teams. Such fatigue may delay care for patients whose alerts are real. Disposition review may give patients some assurance that ignored alerts are examined, though no study measured patient outcomes or trust.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared units with and without disposition logging and review, and none measured patient harm, staff time, or cost. A cluster-randomized or stepped-wedge trial across sites would address this gap if it reported dismissal rates, harm events, and results stratified by payer and language.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One test took place in Tanzania and Rwanda, and two did not report their setting. Health systems serving these groups therefore have no direct evidence on whether disposition review works the same way for their patients.
